name: Bilal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big hydraulic excavator at the Hallam Flats open-cut coal mine, loading the overburden, which is the dirt and rock sitting on top of the coal, into trucks. A good day is when the trucks are lined up, the dipper fills clean and the shift boss leaves me alone. I listen to podcasts on the long stretches, history mostly, and lately a lot about robotics. What wears me out is the twelve hours of sitting, my knees don't love it any more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said robotics podcasts. Is that a new interest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Couple of years now. I use the AI assistant on my phone every day, for the union newsletter I help put together, for my garden, for arguing about history with my son. My wife Lena does bookkeeping part-time and says I'm like a teenager with it. Money's the weak spot, honestly: I sank most of our savings into a dumpling stall at the weekend market three years ago and it folded, so we're starting again from less than a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, actually, because I wanted to see what it could do. At work I'd tease the guys who were scared of it. On the union page I'd post something about how the real fight was always over who owns the machines, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, for me it'd mean the coal clock keeps ticking the same as always. Hallam Flats is meant to wind down in the 2030s anyway, because of climate targets, which I support even if it's my own pit. So my plans stay what they were: work to sixty-three and get out just ahead of the closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on mostly. I'd keep using the assistant for small stuff, and I'd keep putting fifty a week aside to rebuild what the dumpling stall ate. Maybe I'd take a cheap online course in drone surveying anyway, because the mine uses them and I like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed. Like going to the fireworks and they cancel for wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You support the climate targets even though they close your own mine. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got grandkids coming eventually, and I've seen the floods we get now. The pit was never going to last for ever. I'd rather the coal closes with a plan than stays open until the river comes through the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the dumpling stall. What did it teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm better at starting things than at doing the books for them. Lena warned me and I didn't listen. I'd still take a risk again, but a smaller one, with her holding the purse.

S0.say: I'd say it was a shame because I wanted to see what AI could do. I'd post on the union page that the real fight was always about who owns the machines.
S0.think: Privately, it would just mean the coal clock keeps ticking as before, with Hallam Flats due to wind down in the 2030s. My plan stays the same: work to sixty-three and leave just ahead of the closure.
S0.do: Carries on at the excavator and keeps saving fifty a week to rebuild after the failed food stall. Uses his AI assistant for small things and considers a cheap online course in drone surveying.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit disappointed, like fireworks cancelled for wind.
S0.quote: I'd rather the coal closes with a plan than stays open until the river comes through the town.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is the rare miner who is disappointed when AI turns out to be hype. His bigger clock is the coal closure, which he supports on climate grounds despite it ending his own job. The failed dumpling stall explains his thin savings and his new rule of taking smaller risks with his wife holding the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a just transition, where the people who did the hard work get first pick of the new jobs. I'd want the union to bargain for training on full pay, and I'd write it up for the newsletter. Online I'd share the good examples, the mines that kept people on as operators of the new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I could ride this one if I move first. Remote and autonomous excavators need someone watching the screens, and I already know the machine and the computer side a bit. But I'm average, not the best, and I'm fifty-eight, so I'd have to be loud about wanting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask the superintendent straight out what the automation plan is and say I want to be in it. I'd do the drone surveying course, about four hundred, and maybe a remote-operations short course if the union could get it funded. I'd keep the fifty a week going and skip the new phone I was planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the good kind, the kind that gets you out of bed. Mostly I'd be thinking about the money, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'move first'. What happens to the guys who don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that keeps me honest. My mate Tony on the next machine won't touch a smartphone. If I get the screen job and Tony gets the sack, I haven't won anything, I've just been quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Four hundred for a course is a lot from a thin cushion. Would Lena sign off on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would if I showed her the numbers and a job at the end of it. That's the deal since the stall. No proof, no spend.

S1.say: I'd call it the moment for a just transition, where the people who did the hard work get first pick of the new jobs. I'd write up the union's push for training on full pay and share examples of mines that kept their operators on.
S1.think: Off the record, I think I could ride this one if I move first, because remote and automated excavators still need someone watching the screens. But I'm average and fifty-eight, so I'd have to make noise to get chosen.
S1.do: Asks the superintendent about the automation plan in the first month and volunteers to be part of it. Pays about four hundred for a drone surveying course, seeks union funding for a remote-operations course, and skips a planned phone upgrade.
S1.feel: Uneasy in a way that motivates him, with the money worrying him more than the job.
S1.quote: If I get the screen job and Tony gets the sack, I haven't won anything, I've just been quicker.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees opportunity first, but his politics keep pulling him back to colleagues like Tony who won't adapt. His thin savings mean every move has to pass Lena's 'no proof, no spend' rule. The tension between personal advantage and solidarity runs through everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if a machine can do all the work, then the wealth from it has to be shared, a basic income, public ownership of some of it, something. I'd be writing that in every newsletter and I'd be at every rally. This is the fight my whole politics has been about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years is too fast even for me. All my plans, the screen job, the drone course, they assume there's still a human in the loop, and in this picture there isn't. I spent two years learning to talk to the machine, and in this one the machine doesn't need anyone to talk to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still sign up for whatever transition job exists in the first months, because being inside is better than outside. I'd cut the car to one, stop the fifty a week going to the market fund and put it all in the bank. I'd lean on Lena's bookkeeping and maybe pick up books for small businesses with her, using the AI to help, until that goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, to be honest. Not quite hopeless, but I can see the gap between where I am and the pension and nothing to fill it with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough time to be first in the queue, not enough time to build anything. Two years is a sprint and I'm fifty-eight with bad knees. If I had savings it'd be different, but I've got a closed dumpling stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI every day in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more, to understand what's happening and help people with their forms. But it'd feel different. Like using the bulldozer that's knocking down your house to carry your furniture out.

S2.say: I'd say that if machines can do all the work, the wealth has to be shared, through a basic income or public ownership. I'd write it in every newsletter and go to every rally.
S2.think: Privately, two years is too fast even for me, because all my plans assume a human still watching the screens. I'd have spent years learning to talk to the machine and it wouldn't need anyone.
S2.do: Signs up for any transition role in the first months to stay inside the company. Cuts to one car, banks every spare dollar, and starts doing bookkeeping for small businesses with his wife using AI tools.
S2.feel: Alarmed, not hopeless but clearly seeing a gap to the pension with nothing to fill it.
S2.quote: I spent two years learning to talk to the machine, and in this one the machine doesn't need anyone to talk to it.
S2.fieldNote: This is the picture that breaks Bilal's usual optimism, because his adaptability depends on there still being a human role. He responds politically, calling for shared wealth and public ownership, and practically, with a small side business alongside his wife. His bulldozer image captured the feeling of using the tool that is replacing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and the union should be planning now, not reacting. I'd push for a regional transition fund paid by the mining companies. In the newsletter I'd run a column each month on what's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, which was my plan anyway. So if I play it right, I'd ride the change in a remote or training role and step off just as the robots take the last seats. It's tight, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the drone course and push for the remote-operations training. I'd start a proper side thing with Lena, small-business books with AI help, five or six clients by the end of the year. And I'd put the stall loss behind us, a hundred a fortnight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's like a long ramp: you can see the top and you know you might slip, but you're climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between two years and five, in your gut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years I'm reacting. Five years I'm the guy training the robot's first shift and handing it the keys on my way out. That's a much better story to tell my grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you want to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tony, if he'd come. And the young guys on the trucks, who'll still have thirty years of work left to find. I'd want the union to run evening sessions, and I'd teach the AI bits myself if they let me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so the union should start now, not react later. I'd push for a regional transition fund paid by the mining companies and write a monthly column on the changes.
S3.think: Off the record, five years lands me at sixty-three, which was my plan anyway. If I play it right I'd ride the change in a remote or training role and step off as the last seats go.
S3.do: Takes the drone course and pushes for remote-operations training in the first year. Builds a small bookkeeping side business with his wife, aiming for five or six clients, and saves a hundred a fortnight.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but climbing with the top in sight.
S3.quote: Five years I'm the guy training the robot's first shift and handing it the keys on my way out.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Bilal's own retirement timing, which takes the fear out of it. He pictures himself as a bridge, training the machines and the people, and he wants to bring along colleagues who are less keen. The side business with his wife is the clearest sign he learned from the dumpling stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we take it seriously, and a disaster if we don't. Plan the town, plan the pit, plan the people. I'd want the union and the council at the same table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, retired, with luck growing tomatoes. The coal would be closing about then anyway. So for me it's less about my job and more about whether my son and the young ones get something better than the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep learning, and probably end up teaching the AI side to older workers at the union. I'd put the side business with Lena on a proper footing so it carries us past the pension. And I'd tell my son to get into electrical or robotics maintenance, the hands that fix the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, maybe even curious. It feels like something I'd get to watch rather than something that runs me over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'watch'. Do you think you'd miss being part of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want to stay on the union education side after I retire, that's my plan anyway. The work goes but the people still need explaining to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I wasted a lot of money on a dumpling stall, so don't take advice from me on business. But do take it on this. Get a trade the robots need, and don't be the last one to learn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we take it seriously and a disaster if we don't. I'd want the union and the council at the same table planning for the town, the pit and the people.
S4.think: Privately, by 2036 I'm sixty-eight and retired, and the coal would be closing around then anyway. It's less about my job than whether my son and the young ones get something better than the pit.
S4.do: Keeps working and learning, and starts teaching AI basics to older workers through the union. Builds the bookkeeping side business with his wife into a steady income past the pension and pushes his son towards electrical or robotics maintenance.
S4.feel: Calm, even curious, like watching something rather than being run over by it.
S4.quote: Get a trade the robots need, and don't be the last one to learn.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Bilal's retirement and the coal closure roughly line up, so the scenario feels like a story he gets to watch. His adaptability and politics meet in a plan to teach other workers. He remains open about his own past mistake and uses it to make his advice to his son more credible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only picture where being curious doesn't save you. What would help is a real income floor that doesn't depend on being quick, and union-run retraining for people like Tony who'd never sign up on their own. Being early only helps if there's a later to be early for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they lost before this. Half of us already had one pit or mill close on us. We're not new to this, we're tired of it, and nobody ever asks what the last one cost.

headlineQuote: Being early only helps if there's a later to be early for.
portrait: Bilal Zhang is 58 and loads overburden with a big hydraulic excavator at the Hallam Flats coal mine, which is due to close in the 2030s under climate targets he supports. He uses an AI assistant every day, writes for his union newsletter and lost most of his savings on a failed weekend dumpling stall, so he now has under a month in the bank. He's curious and quick to move, calm in the hype picture and only uneasy with steady disruption, where he plans to get into remote operations. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it leaves no human role to adapt into, while five and ten years fit his own retirement. Throughout, he keeps pulling the conversation back to colleagues who won't adapt and to who owns the machines.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it's the only one where being curious and quick doesn't save him.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor that doesn't depend on being quick, and union-run retraining for workers who wouldn't sign up on their own.
